sections.title: Comparison of Shareholder Rights
text: Prospective investors should be aware that the Bermuda Companies Act, which applies to us, differs in certain material respects from laws generally applicable to U.S. companies incorporated in the State of Delaware and their shareholders. The following is a summary of certain significant differences between the Bermuda Companies Act (including modifications adopted pursuant to our Amended and Restated Bye-Laws) and Bermuda common law applicable to us and our shareholders, on the one hand, and the provisions of the Delaware General Corporation Law applicable to U.S. companies organized under the laws of Delaware and their shareholders, on the other hand.

The Bermuda Companies Act authorizes the directors of a company, subject to its bye-laws, to exercise all powers of the company except those that are required by the Bermuda Companies Act or the company’s bye-laws to be exercised by the shareholders of the company. sections.title: Note 7. Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
text: FASB ASC 820-10, Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures, defines fair value, establishes a consistent framework for measuring fair value and requires disclosures about fair value measurements. The standard requires the Group to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs when measuring fair value.

FASB ASC 820-10 specifies a hierarchy of inputs based on whether the inputs are observable or unobservable. Observable inputs are developed using market data and reflect market participant assumptions, while unobservable inputs reflect the Group’s market assumptions. The fair value hierarchy is as follows:
•Level 1 — observable inputs such as quoted prices for identical assets in active markets;
•Level 2 — inputs other than quoted prices for identical assets in active markets, that are observable either directly or indirectly; and
•Level 3 — unobservable inputs in which there is little or no market data which requires the use of valuation techniques and the development of assumptions

As required under the fair value hierarchy, the Group considers relevant and observable market inputs in its valuations where possible. The frequency of transactions, the size of the bid-ask spread and the amount of adjustment necessary when comparing similar transactions are all factors in determining the liquidity of markets and the relevance of observable prices in those markets.
The Group’s policy with respect to transfer between levels of the fair value hierarchy is to recognize transfers into and out of each level as of the end of the reporting period.

The effective rates for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026 were 14.9% and 15.0% respectively, compared to 11.9% and 17.6% for the three and six months ended June 30, 2025.

The difference between the effective tax rate on income from continuing operations and the U.K. statutory rate of 25% is primarily because of income recognized in jurisdictions with lower tax rates than the United Kingdom, and adjustments pursuant to applicable U.S. GAAP guidance on interim financial reporting of taxes, which are based on the annual estimated effective tax rate.

In arriving at the estimated annual effective tax rate for the six months ended June 30, 2026 and 2025, the Company took into consideration all year-to-date income and expense items including the change in unrealized investment gains (losses) and realized investment gains (losses) and such items on a forecasted basis for the remainder of each year. The Company's income tax expense may fluctuate from period to period based on the relative mix of income or loss reported by jurisdiction and the varying tax rates in each jurisdiction.

Recognition of the benefit of a given tax position is based upon whether a company determines that it is more likely than not that a tax position will be sustained upon examination based upon the technical merits of the position. In evaluating the more likely than not recognition threshold, the Company must presume that the tax position will be subject to examination by a taxing authority with full knowledge of all relevant information. …

sections.title: Note 14. Debt
text: On December 3, 2022, the Group entered into a Credit and Guaranty Agreement (“Credit Facility”) for a 7-year term loan facility (“Term Loan Facility”), with periodic interest and quarterly principal payments and 5.0% base rate spread, which was due to mature on January 3, 2030. Interest was payable in three month intervals after the first interest payment date of July 31, 2023.

The Term Loan Facility was drawn on January 3, 2023. The original principal of the term loan was $1,175.0 million and issuances costs were $20.2 million. As of December 31, 2023, $1,172.1 million of the principal was outstanding, $23.2 million of interest was accrued, and the related unamortized deferred issuance costs were $37.2 million.

On October 17, 2024, the Group refinanced the 7-year Term Loan Facility. As at October 17, 2024, the original 7-year Term Loan Facility principal was $1,163.3 million, which was settled and replaced with a new $2,000.0 million 7-year Term Loan Facility with periodic interest and quarterly principal payments and 4.00% base rate spread (subject to adjustment in certain circumstances), which will mature on October 17, 2031. Interest is payable in three month intervals after the first interest payment date of March 31, 2025. On settlement and replacement of the original 7-year Term Loan Facility unamortized deferred issuance costs of $37.2 million were expensed and $20.2 million of debt issuance costs from the new 7-year Term Loan Facility were deferred.
As of December 31, 2025, $1,980.0 million of the principal was outstanding, $7.2 million of interest was accrued, and the related unamortized deferred issuance costs were $16.2 million.
As of June 30, 2026, $1,970.0 million of the principal was outstanding, $9.9 million of interest was accrued, and the related unamortized deferred issuance costs were $14.4 million.

text: From time to time in the normal course of business, the Group may be involved in formal and informal dispute resolution procedures, which may include arbitration or litigation, the outcomes of which determine the rights and obligations of the Group under the Group’s contractual agreements, or other matters as the case may be. In some disputes, the Group may seek to enforce its rights under an agreement or to collect funds owing to it. In other

matters, the Group may resist attempts by others to collect funds or enforce alleged rights. revenue.heading: Revenue Recognition
revenue.text:
We generate revenue from providing insurance services to our clients and incur costs in providing these services primarily through employee compensation, property costs and other costs associated with the tools, systems and applications that are required to deliver these services. While most of our efforts and costs are incurred providing pre-placement services for underwriting origination, pricing, and negotiation, some services and costs are required to support the post placement obligations including claims handling, credit control, and policy administration. Accordingly, we defer some of our revenue to be recognized over the period that these post-placement activities are performed.

Placement commission is recognized when a policy is bound and issued, and the estimation thereof includes certain estimates for the timing of underlying attachments for certain types of insurance and reinsurance contracts such as business written through quota share reinsurance contracts or aggregate lineslips. Additionally, certain insurance policies contain cancellation clauses. For these contracts, placement commission estimates are recognized after taking into consideration future cancellations based upon our historical experience.
